activities.anchor: Einstein's 1905 theory rests on a clash
activities.caption: assemble the clash that forced the postulate
activities.name: srClashOrder

config.prompt: Build the argument step by step:
items: Principle of relativity: physics works identically in every laboratory moving at constant velocity — you cannot feel cruise motion
Maxwell's electromagnetism predicts light travels at c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s — but relative to what? The nineteenth-century answer: the ether
Michelson–Morley (1887) compares light speeds along different directions hunting Earth's motion through the ether — and finds nothing
Einstein takes the null result at face value as a postulate: light moves at c for every inertial observer
config.why: Keep that postulate and something else you believed — that time is universal — has to go.

activities.anchor: the light from both arrives at the ground observer together
activities.caption: true or false — lightning and the moving train
activities.name: srTrainJudge

statements.s: The passenger at the train's centre is moving toward the front bolt's light and away from the rear's.
statements.why: So the front light reaches her first — she concludes the front bolt struck first.

statements.s: Both light beams travel at c for the passenger too.
statements.why: The postulate applies to her as much as to the ground observer — that is what forces the disagreement.

statements.s: Simultaneity is a property of the events themselves.
statements.why: It is a property of the frame — both observers are right, and neither is 'more correct'.

statements.s: No observer ever sees an effect precede its cause, provided causes cannot outrun light.
statements.why: The disagreement is bounded — causal order is protected, which is what makes the relativity livable.

activities.caption: file each quantity — frame-dependent or agreed by all
activities.name: srFrameSort

config.prompt: Not everything is relative — file each quantity:

items.label: whether the two lightning bolts were simultaneous
the reading a moving clock shows compared across frames
an object's length along its direction of motion
the order of events a signal could connect
causal order — no effect ever precedes its cause

config.why: Distant simultaneity is frame-dependent; causal order is protected by the light-speed limit — that is the correct picture.

activities.anchor: created by cosmic rays at ~15 km altitude
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — clocks on airliners
activities.name: srHafeleEst

config.prompt: Hafele and Keating (1971) flew caesium clocks around the world on airliners. How much did the eastward-flying clock lose relative to the US Naval Observatory?
config.why: The eastward clock lost ~59 ns and the westward gained ~273 ns — matching the combined special- and general-relativistic predictions to within error bars.
config.context: The same bookkeeping corrects the clock in your phone hourly — relativity is engineering-grade, not museum-grade.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the paired effect
activities.name: srContractCloze

config.text: Length contraction is the paired effect: L = L₀/%%0%%, where L₀ is the rest length — and only the motion direction shrinks, so a relativistic spaceship is shorter but not thinner. At everyday speeds the effect is real but unmeasurable: a jet at 250 m/s loses about a %%1%% across the whole aircraft.
config.hint: The first blank is the same multiplier that slows moving clocks; the second is a tiny unit of length.

activities.anchor: if two observers each see the other's clock run slow
activities.caption: find the faulty line in this student's twin-paradox notes
activities.name: srTwinSpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's twin-paradox notes is wrong — click it:
lines: Each observer sees the other's clock run slow — no contradiction, because they also disagree about simultaneity.
The travelling twin returns younger — by both accounts, unambiguously.
The asymmetry that resolves the case: the stay-at-home twin changes frames at turnaround.
The travelling twin accelerates at turnaround, so the two are not interchangeable.
Verified with clocks on airliners and particles in storage rings, slowed by γ factors of thousands.
config.correction: It is the travelling twin who changes frames (accelerates at turnaround) — that asymmetry is why the traveller ages less.
config.why: The full calculation with both effects agrees: the traveller ages less. 'Compare two separated clocks' secretly depends on which events count as simultaneous.

activities.caption: which curve is the relativistic sum?
activities.name: srAddTrace

config.prompt: A ship moves at speed v (fraction of c) and fires a projectile at 0.9c relative to itself. Which curve is the speed a stationary observer measures?
config.xlabel: ship speed v (in units of c)
config.ylabel: measured projectile speed u (in units of c)
config.why: The denominator bends velocity space so that c is the asymptote: 0.9c + 0.9c gives 1.8/1.81 ≈ 0.9945c, and light added to anything still gives exactly c.

activities.caption: pair each mass–energy ledger entry with its number
activities.name: srLedgerMatch

config.prompt: One ledger, four entries — pair each with its figure:

pairs.right: converts ~4 million tonnes of mass to radiance every second
9 × 10¹³ J — about 25 gigawatt-hours, a large power plant's day
weighs 0.7% less than the four protons that fuse to make it — that deficit is sunlight
create mass, turning kinetic energy into new particles whose rest mass comes entirely from collision energy

config.why: Mass is not consumed while energy appears: mass IS an energy account, and the single mass–energy ledger always balances.
